runs.t: Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I
Study file | Source: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8.0 RH124 workbook

This chapter teaches you how to get a shell prompt on a Linux system and how to type simple commands quickly. You will log in at the console, on the desktop and over the network. Then you will use bash shortcuts to save time.
Accessing the Command Line Using the Desktop
Executing Commands Using the Bash Shell
1.1 What the shell and bash are
The shell gives you a command line, and bash is the shell Red Hat Enterprise Linux uses by default.
is a text screen where you type instructions to the computer. The program that provides it is called the
. Think of a receptionist who takes your written request and passes it on (the shell is also a small programming language). The default shell is
, the GNU Bourne-Again Shell, an improved version of the older Bourne Shell (
Bash is similar in idea to the Windows command prompt (
) and to Windows PowerShell, but its scripting language is more advanced.
Bash is the default shell in macOS.
Starting with macOS Catalina, new user accounts use zsh as the default shell. Bash was the default in macOS Mojave and earlier.

The shell runs what you type, and bash is the shell you will use in this course.
The prompt shows that the shell is ready, and its last character tells you whether you are a normal user or root.

Every command you type has up to three parts: the command, its options and its arguments.

You reach a shell through a terminal, and one computer can offer several terminals at once.

Think of one TV with six channels: each shows something different, and a key combination changes the channel. Press Ctrl+Alt and a function key from F1 to F6 at the same time to switch. The comparison stops here: every console keeps running while you watch another. Most show a text login prompt. Log in correctly and you get a shell prompt.
Where to run it: at the computer's own keyboard and display (not over ssh). Changes: only which console you see. Undo: press the combination for the console you left.

Each console has its own login session, separate from the others.

1.5 The graphical login and its console
In RHEL 8, the graphical login runs on console 1, and your desktop starts on the next free console, normally console 2.
If a graphical environment is available, the login screen runs on the first virtual console, called
. Five more text login prompts wait on consoles two to six. After you log in graphically, your desktop starts on the first console not used by a login session, normally

Think of a hotel: reception is always on the first floor, and your room is on the next free floor. If console 2 holds an active text login, the desktop takes the next free console. A second graphical user, or Switch User, gets another free console. The comparison stops here: a console is a screen, not a floor. When you log out, the display returns to the login screen on tty1.
Where to run it: at the computer's own keyboard and display. Changes: only which console your desktop uses.
1. Log in at the graphical login screen (console 1).
The display returns to the login screen on console 1.

Consoles two to six: text logins, when they are free.
Many administrators do not run a graphical environment on servers. This leaves the resources free for the server's services.
In RHEL 6 and 7, your desktop replaces the login screen on console 1. In RHEL 5 and earlier, consoles 1 to 6 were always text logins, and the desktop ran on console 7 (Ctrl+Alt+F7).
The book describes the RHEL 8 layout: login screen on tty1, desktop on tty2.

NOT VERIFIED for current RHEL versions. To check on your own system: log in to the desktop, then press Ctrl+Alt+F1, then Ctrl+Alt+F2, and see which console shows the login screen and which shows your desktop.
The login screen stays on tty1; your desktop starts on the next free console.
1.6 Headless servers and the serial console
A headless server has no permanent keyboard or display, so you reach it over the network or, in an emergency, a serial console.
to save space and money. A

is a login prompt on a serial port, wired to a networked console server for remote access. It is mostly used to fix a server whose network card is misconfigured, because normal network login is then impossible. Most of the time you reach headless servers over the network.
The serial console is the emergency door; the network is the normal door.
1.7 Logging in over the network with SSH
SSH gives you a shell on a remote machine over an encrypted network connection.
Many servers are virtual machines or cloud instances with no real console, so you log in over the network. The usual tool is
command from OpenSSH is available on Red Hat Enterprise Linux and macOS.

Think of a sealed armoured car carrying your messages: nobody on the road can read or change what is inside. The comparison stops here: the car protects the trip, not the server at the end. The ssh command encrypts the connection to protect your password and content from eavesdropping and hijacking.
Where to run it: on host, as user. Changes: nothing, apart from starting a login session. Check: the prompt shows remoteuser@remotehost. Undo: type exit.
: the command that opens the remote login.
: the account on the remote machine.
: the name of the remote machine.
stands for the password you type.
ssh user@host opens an encrypted shell on a remote machine.
1.8 Logging in with a key instead of a password
Public key login lets you enter a remote machine with a private key file instead of a password.
Some systems, such as new cloud instances, do not allow password logins with ssh. Instead you use
. You keep an identity file that holds a
, which is equal to a password and must stay secret. Your account on the server holds the matching
, which does not have to be secret.

Think of a lock and a key. The lock (public key) can hang where everyone sees it, but only your key (private key) opens it. The comparison stops here: a key file can be copied, so only you may read it.

Where to run it: on host, as user. The matching public key must already be set up in the remoteuser account. Changes: the first command changes the key file's permissions. Check: no password is asked. Undo: type exit.
: the option that names the private key (identity) file to use.
: the private key file in this example.
: makes the key file readable only by its owner (file permissions are taught in a later chapter).
A private key is like a password: keep it secret and readable only by you.
ssh asks you once to trust a new server, and it warns you if that server's key later changes.
Each time you connect, the remote host sends its

to prove who it is. The first time, ssh has no saved key for it, so it shows a warning and asks you to decide. Think of a passport check: on the first visit you accept the passport and note it down; on later visits ssh compares it with your note.

Host keys are unique for each server. They need to be changed periodically, and whenever a compromise is suspected.
The example shows the fingerprint as hex pairs with colons (47:bf:82:...).

Say yes only to a host you trust; a changed key later is a warning sign.

Accessing the Command Line Using the Desktop
The desktop is the graphical interface, and RHEL 8 uses GNOME 3 with the "Standard" theme.
is the graphical interface of a Linux system. In RHEL 8 it is
, which runs on a display system called Wayland (by default) or the older X Window System.
provides the core screens and menus.

Think of a car dashboard: one panel that puts the controls within reach. RHEL 8 uses the "Standard" theme. RHEL 7 used the "Classic" theme. On your first login, a setup program runs, then the GNOME Help application opens on a Getting Started screen.
Where to run it: at the graphical login screen. Changes: the theme of your login sessions.
2. Click the gear icon next to the Sign In button.
3. Pick Standard or Classic, enter your password, and sign in.
The desktop starts with the theme you picked.
: the default display system in RHEL 8.

GNOME 3 runs on Wayland by default, or on the older X Window System.

RHEL 9 deprecated the Xorg server, and RHEL 10 removed it. Wayland is the display stack, and Xwayland remains for older X11 applications. CentOS Stream 10, the upstream of RHEL 10, ships GNOME 47. Your RHEL 8 lab still matches the book.

GNOME Shell is the desktop you see; Wayland or X draws it on screen.
2.2 The top bar and the Activities overview
The top bar runs along the top of the screen, and the Activities overview is the mode for starting applications and organising windows.
holds the Activities button and controls for volume, network, the calendar and keyboard input methods. The

in the upper-right corner adjusts screen brightness, switches network connections, and opens Settings. It also locks the screen and shuts the system down, and its user-name submenu has account settings and log out.
Think of the home button on a phone: one press shows everything you can do. The
opens when you click Activities (upper left) or press the
, also called the Windows key or Command key. Click Activities again, or press Super or Esc, to leave without doing anything.
Where to run it: at the desktop. Changes: only the view. Undo: press Esc.
The Activities overview opens, with the dash on the left, windows in the centre and workspaces on the right.
: the strip at the top of the screen.

Super (or the Activities button) opens the overview; Esc closes it.
2.3 The dash, windows overview and workspace selector
The Activities overview has three areas: the dash, the windows overview and the workspace selector.
is on the left. It lists your favourite applications and running applications, with a grid button at the bottom to find any other application. It is also called the dock. The
is in the centre. It shows thumbnails of all windows in the current workspace, so you can bring one to the front or move it to another workspace. The
is on the right. It shows thumbnails of all workspaces.
Think of a shop: a shelf of favourites on the left, a table showing everything you are working on in the middle, and a floor map on the right.
Where to run it: at the desktop, in the Activities overview. Changes: only the view.
Click the grid button at the bottom of the dash.
A grid of applications appears, including less common ones.
Dash on the left, windows in the centre, workspaces on the right.
2.4 The message tray and keyboard shortcuts
The message tray shows your notifications, and GNOME keyboard shortcuts can be viewed and changed in Settings.
When a notification arrives, it first appears briefly as one line at the top of the screen. Then a persistent indicator appears next to the clock. Click the clock, or press Super+M, to open the
. Close it with the clock, Esc, or Super+M again. Think of a mailbox by the front door that fills up while you are busy.
To view or edit your shortcuts, open the system menu, click Settings, then choose Devices, then Keyboard.
Where to run it: at the desktop. Changes: only the view. Undo: press Esc.
The message tray opens and lists recent notifications.
: opens or closes the message tray (in the book's RHEL 8 desktop).

Some shortcuts, such as function keys or the Super key, can be hard to send to a virtual machine. Your local operating system, or the application you use to view the desktop, may capture those keystrokes.

The current GNOME Help page lists Super+V to show the notification list, and Super+L to lock the screen. Which GNOME release made this change is NOT VERIFIED. To check on your system, open Settings and look at the Keyboard shortcuts.

2.5 Sending special keys in a browser-based classroom
In a virtual classroom, your browser may not pass special keys like Super to the machine, so an on-screen keyboard can send them.

In Red Hat's virtual and self-paced training environments, the Super key is usually not passed to the virtual machine by your web browser. The classroom provides an on-screen keyboard instead. Open it with the keyboard icon on the right of the bar at the top of the browser window, and click the icon again to close it.
Think of a remote control that has no "volume" button: you use the screen menu instead. On the on-screen keyboard,
are held down by clicking them once. To send Super+M, click Super, then click M.

The message tray opens, as if you pressed Super+M.

In Red Hat's current training environments, the Super key is usually not passed through the browser. Use the on-screen keyboard. It treats Super, Shift, Ctrl, Alt and Caps as hold keys: click once to hold (the key turns yellow), click again to release.
The on-screen keyboard is in the Ravello Systems bar of the browser window.

If a shortcut does not work in a browser classroom, use the on-screen keyboard.
Workspaces are separate desktop screens that let you group windows by task.
has its own application windows. For example, keep the windows for a server setup in one workspace and your email in another. Think of having two desks: one for the job, one for everything else.

The fastest way to switch is Ctrl+Alt+UpArrow or Ctrl+Alt+DownArrow, which moves through the workspaces in order. The other way is the Activities overview: click the workspace you want. The overview also lets you drag a window between workspaces, using the windows overview and the workspace selector.
Where to run it: at the desktop, with at least two workspaces in use. Changes: only which workspace you see. Undo: press the opposite arrow.
The screen switches to the next workspace.

In Red Hat's training environments, Ctrl+Alt combinations are usually not passed through the browser. With the on-screen keyboard, click Ctrl, Alt, then UpArrow or DownArrow. At least two workspaces must be in use. It is simpler to click Activities, then click the workspace in the selector.
Ctrl+Alt+Up or Down switches workspaces, or click one in the Activities overview.
To get a shell prompt on the desktop, start a graphical terminal such as GNOME Terminal.

There are two common ways. First, open the Activities overview and choose Terminal in the dash (in the favourites, in the Utilities group under the grid button, or by typing in the search field). Second, press Alt+F2 to open the Enter a Command box, and type
Think of the terminal window as a window into the shell. The prompt and the window's title bar show your user name, the host name and the working directory.
Where to run it: at the desktop, as your own user. Changes: opens a window. Undo: type exit, or close the window.
A terminal window opens with a prompt like [user@host ~]$

2.8 Locking, logging out and powering off
The system menu in the top bar locks the screen, logs you out, or shuts the computer down.

the screen, click the lock button in the system menu or press Super+L. The screen also locks after the session is idle for a few minutes. To unlock, press Enter or Space to raise the lock screen curtain, then enter your password. To
, open the system menu, choose your name, then Log Out, and confirm.

Think of the three as: stepping away (lock), leaving the room (log out) and switching off the building (power off). To power off, click the power button in the system menu or press Ctrl+Alt+Del, then choose Power Off, Restart or Cancel. With no choice, the system shuts down after 60 seconds.
Where to run it: at the desktop. Changes: only the screen is locked. Undo: unlock with your password.
A lock screen shows the system time and your user name.
Lock to step away, log out to end your session, power off to shut the machine down.

Executing Commands Using the Bash Shell
Each line you type has a command, options and arguments, and you press Enter to run it.
A command is the name of a program installed on the system. Each command has its own options and arguments. Separate every word with a space, and type each command on its own line. When you press
, the command runs, and its output appears before the next prompt.
Think of handing a note to a clerk: the answer comes back before you hand over the next note.
Where to run it: any host, as a normal user. Changes: nothing.
: a command with no options and no arguments. It prints the user name.
The new prompt: the shell is ready for the next command.
One command per line; press Enter and read the output.

A semicolon lets you type more than one command on a single line.
: a character with a special meaning to bash. Here it separates commands. The shell runs them one after another and shows the output of both before the next prompt.
Think of writing two errands on one note, with a semicolon between them. The comparison stops here: the shell does not skip the second one when the first has a problem; it just goes on.
Where to run it: any host, as a normal user. Changes: nothing (the commands only read). The wc command is explained in 3.9.

3.11 Continuing a long command on another line
A backslash at the end of a line lets one command continue on the next line.
Bash scrolls long commands for you, but they can be hard to read. Add a backslash
as the very last character on a line. It tells the shell to ignore the newline and treat the next line as part of the same command. You can do this more than once.

3.13 Arrow keys and Alt+. for earlier commands
The arrow keys let you recall and edit earlier commands, and Alt+. pastes the last word of the previous command.
UpArrow brings back the previous command from the history, and DownArrow brings the next one. LeftArrow and RightArrow move the cursor within the command, so you can edit it before pressing Enter.

, to insert the last word of the previous command at the cursor. Press it again to replace that word with the last word of an even earlier command. Alt+. is handy because you can hold Alt and tap the dot repeatedly. Think of a stack of notes you flip through one by one.
Where to run it: any host, in a terminal. Changes: nothing until you press Enter.
[user@host ~]$ ls      (type ls and a space, then press Alt+.)

Arrow keys recall commands; Alt+. reuses the last word.
